newsitem.title: UK: UK budget to forecast steady growth, low inflation.
newsitem.headline: UK budget to forecast steady growth, low inflation.

text.p: British Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's first budget will be delivered against an unusually promising background of a buoyant economy, muted inflation and fairly healthy public finances.

Although the Labour finance minister has asked the National Audit Office to review the economic assumptions on which the budget is based, economists expect little change in the economic outlook he will paint.
Former Conservative Chancellor Kenneth Clarke's last budget in November 1996 forecast a "Goldilocks Recovery."

Clarke's Red Book, which lays out the budget and Treasury economic forecasts in full, tipped economic growth of 3.5 percent in 1997, consumer spending up 4.25 percent over the year, underlying inflation falling to 2.5 percent by the year-end and a public sector borrowing requirement (budget deficit) of 19.2 billion pounds for fiscal 1997/98.
"I wouldn't have thought the overall tenor of the forecasts would change much," said John Shepperd, chief economist at Yamaichi International.

Underlying inflation, excluding home loan payments, would probably be below 2.5 percent by the end of the year and while the existing growth and high street spending forecasts may look a little optimistic, they are not overly so.
"It will be more fine-tuning the numbers than starting with a blank sheet of paper -- changes only well after the decimal point," Shepperd said.
In fact, consumer spending growth may yet match or exceed forecasts, with Britain's building societies showering millions of members with shares as they convert into banks.

Economists estimate a total of about 30 billion pounds in shares will be paid out this summer, with a quarter or more of that likely to be spent immediately. To put that in context, a one penny income tax cut pumps about 1.5 billion pounds into the economy.

Halifax, Britain's largest mortgage lender, floated on Monday and saw its shares rocket to nearly eight pounds each. That alone equates to more than 17 billion pounds in shares paid into consumers' pockets.
Last week, U.S. investment bank Goldman Sachs and the Institute for Fiscal Studies forecast consumer spending growth at 4.3 percent this year, with GDP growth of 3.2 percent.
In their "Green Budget", which is traditionally released as a precursor to the real thing, they said real take-home pay has risen by more than three percent over the last year.

"In addition, consumer confidence is being boosted by a recovering housing market, falling unemployment and a substantial amount of windfalls from takeovers and stock market flotations of building socities and insurance companies."

That, within the larger picture of buoyant domestic demand, is what is worrying the Bank of England and has many economists hoping Brown will produce a tight budget to take the heat out of high street spending.
But with Britain's public sector deficit set to undercut forecasts by a hefty amount, Brown is under no pressure on that front to raise taxes.
As he has promised to live within existing public spending limits, he has two choices -- accept the lower budget deficit as a bonus or use some of the proceeds to cut taxes.

Clarke's Red Book forecast a PSBR of 19.2 billion stg this year. But the total deficit for last year, at 23.1 billion stg, came in more than three billion pounds below target and economists expect further improvement in the current year.

"Fifteen billion seems a sensible figure for the PSBR given last year's undercut and the April figures we have already seen," Shepperd said, referring to April figures which showed an unexpected debt repayment. The IFS/Goldman Green Budget forecast a PSBR of 14.3 billion pounds.
Michael Saunders, UK economist at Salomon Brothers, is even more optimistic about Britain's public debt, forecasting only a 13 billion shortfall this year if policy is left unchanged.
That would leave Britain's new Chancellor tantalisingly close to achieving his "golden rule" -- borrowing only to invest so the fiscal deficit does not exceed net capital spending.
"Only a further modest tightening is needed to meet Mr Brown's golden rule target next year," Saunders said. "The structural deficit is not large enough to justify big tax hikes."
Shepperd agreed. "There's nothing unduly worrying about the sort of PSBR we are talking about, even at this stage of the economic cycle."
